lead: Green's theorem turns a line integral around a closed plane curve into a double integral over the region inside it. For a curve C that runs anticlockwise and a region R, the integral of M dx + N dy along C equals the integral of ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y over R. The theorem saves work when the boundary has many pieces. It also gives area formulas and shows when a line integral depends only on endpoints.
prereq: You need line integrals from 6.4 and double integrals over rectangles and triangles from Unit 5, Multiple Integrals.

blocks.text: Let R be a closed plane region with boundary C. Let M(x,y) and N(x,y) have continuous first partial derivatives on R and on C. If C is piecewise smooth, closed, and taken anticlockwise, then the line integral and the double integral are equal.

blocks.where: M and N are functions of x and y; C is the anticlockwise boundary of R; dA is the area element dx dy; the left side is a line integral round C and the right side is a double integral over R.

blocks.text: Positive orientation means this: walk along C in the chosen direction. The region R stays on your left. For a simple rectangle, that is anticlockwise: bottom edge left to right, right edge upward, top edge right to left, left edge downward.

The curve may have corners. A triangle or a rectangle is fine. Split a cornered curve into smooth pieces and add the line integrals. The statement needs C closed. An open curve cannot be used directly.

sections.h3: Two uses and the area formula

blocks.text: Most exam questions use the theorem forward. The line integral has many edges and awkward limits. The double integral has one region and simpler limits. Compute ∂N/∂x and ∂M/∂y first. Keep the order: N first, then M.

Use it backward when you want an area. Pick M and N so that ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y = 1. Then the double integral is just the area of R. One choice is M = −y/2 and N = x/2. Check: ∂N/∂x = 1/2 and ∂M/∂y = −1/2, so the difference is 1. Green's theorem then gives the area formula.
A = ∬<sub>R</sub> dA = ½ ∮<sub>C</sub> (x dy − y dx)
blocks.where: A is the area of R; C is the anticlockwise boundary; x and y are the coordinates on C.

blocks.text: Another choice is M = 0 and N = x. Then A = ∮<sub>C</sub> x dy. The formula A = ½∮(x dy − y dx) is symmetric and often easier on a circle.

The theorem still holds when R has a hole. Let C2 be the outer boundary and C1 the inner boundary. Orient C2 anticlockwise and C1 clockwise. Then R stays on the left on both curves. The formula becomes ∮<sub>C2</sub> + ∮<sub>C1</sub> = ∬<sub>R</sub> (∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y) dA.
For a hole, a common mistake is to orient both boundaries anticlockwise. That leaves the hole on the left for the inner curve, so the sign is wrong. Draw an arrow on each boundary before you compute.

If you reverse the direction of C, every dx and dy changes sign. The line integral changes sign, and the double integral does not. So a clockwise curve gives the negative of the anticlockwise answer. State the orientation in your answer.
Continuity matters. If M or N or a first partial derivative blows up inside R, do not apply the theorem across that point. Cut a small circle around the bad point and take a limit.

figure.caption: The chain runs from the plane region R to its anticlockwise boundary C, then to the line integral, which equals the double integral of ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y over R. The last arrow is the theorem.

spec.title: Green's theorem in one line
spec.aria: A left-to-right chain from a plane region to its anticlockwise boundary curve, then to the line integral, which equals the double integral of Nx minus My over R.

examples.question: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ∮<sub>C</sub> (x<sup>2</sup> − y<sup>2</sup>) dx + 2xy dy, where C is the boundary of the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, taken anticlockwise.
steps: Compare with ∮(M dx + N dy). Here M = x² − y² and N = 2xy.
The region is the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1. Apply Green: ∮ = ∬<sub>R</sub> 4y dA = ∫₀² ∫₀¹ 4y dy dx.

Check by the line integral. Bottom edge y = 0, dy = 0, x from 0 to 2: ∫ x² dx = 8/3. Right edge x = 2, dx = 0, y from 0 to 1: ∫ 4y dy = 2. Top edge y = 1, x from 2 to 0: ∫ (x² − 1) dx = −2/3. Left edge x = 0, dx = 0, y from 1 to 0: integral is 0. Sum = 8/3 + 2 − 2/3 + 0 = 4.
examples.answer: The value of the line integral is 4.

from fractions import Fraction
inner = Fraction(4, 1) * Fraction(1, 2)
total = inner * 2
print(int(total))

traps: Writing ∂M/∂y − ∂N/∂x instead of ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y. The sign of the double integral flips.
Using a clockwise curve but forgetting that the line integral changes sign.
Applying the theorem to a curve that is not closed. Close it with an extra segment, apply the theorem, then subtract the extra integral.
Mixing the coefficients M and N. M multiplies dx and N multiplies dy.
For a region with a hole, giving both boundaries the same orientation. The inner boundary must be clockwise for the outer boundary anticlockwise.

quiz.q: State Green's theorem for a plane region R with anticlockwise boundary C.
quiz.a: ∮<sub>C</sub> (M dx + N dy) = ∬<sub>R</sub> (∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y) dA, when M and N have continuous first partial derivatives on R.

quiz.q: Why is the anticlockwise direction used in the standard statement?
quiz.a: Anticlockwise keeps the region R on the left as you walk along C. This is positive orientation. A clockwise curve gives the negative value.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∮<sub>C</sub> x dy, where C is the anticlockwise boundary of the unit square 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1.
quiz.a: M = 0, N = x. Then ∂N/∂x = 1 and ∂M/∂y = 0. The double integral is ∬<sub>R</sub> 1 dA = area = 1. So the line integral is 1.

quiz.q: Use A = ½∮<sub>C</sub> (x dy − y dx) for the circle x = a cos t, y = a sin t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Find the area.
quiz.a: dx = −a sin t dt, dy = a cos t dt. Then x dy − y dx = a²(cos²t + sin²t) dt = a² dt. So A = ½∫₀²π a² dt = πa².

quiz.q: R is an annulus between an outer circle C2 and an inner circle C1. How do you orient C1 and why?
quiz.a: Orient C2 anticlockwise and C1 clockwise. Then the region R stays on the left on both curves. Add the two line integrals to get the double integral over R.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∮<sub>C</sub> (y dx + x dy) around any closed anticlockwise curve.
quiz.a: M = y and N = x. Then ∂N/∂x = 1 and ∂M/∂y = 1. The difference is 0, so the double integral is 0. The line integral is 0.

quiz.q: Can you apply Green's theorem directly to a curve that is not closed? What do you do instead?
quiz.a: No. Green's theorem needs a closed boundary. Add an extra segment to close the curve, apply the theorem to the closed curve, then subtract the line integral along the extra segment.

beyond: Not for the exam. Green's theorem is the plane version of Stokes' theorem and of the divergence theorem. In complex analysis it proves Cauchy's integral theorem for analytic functions. In engineering it underlies finite element methods for heat and stress in flat plates. Search next: Green's theorem complex analysis, planimeter, finite element weak form.
